title: Starting a Hospice Program in Minnesota: Licensing, Costs, and Step-by-Step Guide

html:
Introduction (2-3 paragraphs)

Starting a Hospice Program in Minnesota represents a meaningful opportunity to serve individuals with terminal illnesses requiring end-of-life care while building a compliant, sustainable care business. Oversight and funding are administered by the Minnesota Department of Health (MDH), which is the primary state licensing body. Reimbursement and program funding are coordinated through federal and state payers, primarily Medicare and Minnesota’s Medicaid program (Medical Assistance).

With moderate opportunity for new providers and reimbursement rates like Medicare’s $210-$350 per day, Minnesota offers a moderately competitive market with significant opportunities for providers offering specialized services and residential care. The state has approximately 100 licensed providers, but there are localized capacity pressures and a growing need for niche services, including pediatric hospice, residential facilities, and specialized dementia care. Success hinges on a provider’s ability to navigate the state’s licensing process, build a qualified interdisciplinary team, and establish strong referral relationships.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Hospice Program in Minnesota, from understanding the regulations under Minnesota Statutes sections 144A.75 to navigating licensing, staffing, reimbursement, and preparing for state and federal inspections. Whether you are an experienced healthcare professional or an entrepreneur with a passion for compassionate care, this comprehensive overview will provide the roadmap you need to get started.

Table of Contents

  • Understand Minnesota’s Hospice Program Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand Minnesota’s Hospice Program Regulations

Minnesota regulates Hospice Programs through the Minnesota Department of Health (MDH), which is responsible for licensing and oversight of hospice programs under Minnesota Statutes sections 144A.75, ensuring compliance with state regulations for patient care, safety, and quality. This statute, along with its associated rules, forms the foundation of your compliance obligations. Providers serving the vast majority of the eligible population must also comply with federal frameworks, most notably the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Conditions of Participation (CoPs) for hospice care, and the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) for patient privacy.

The regulatory framework in Minnesota emphasizes interdisciplinary team-based care, patient and family rights, pain and symptom management, and comprehensive care planning. The core of hospice is the Interdisciplinary Group (IDG), which must develop and review each patient’s plan of care. This focus ensures that care is holistic, addressing not just the physical needs of the patient but also their emotional, social, and spiritual well-being. Licenses are subject to renewal, typically on an annual or biennial basis, contingent on maintaining compliance and passing any required inspections.

Navigating the interplay between MDH state rules and the federal CMS Conditions of Participation is one of the most critical challenges for a new hospice agency. While there is significant overlap, there are distinct requirements from each body that must be met. For example, both mandate specific compositions for the IDG and timelines for care planning, but documentation standards or survey processes may differ. A deep understanding of both sets of rules is non-negotiable for licensure, certification, and long-term operational success.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

Minnesota supports multiple levels of hospice care, which are defined by CMS and reimbursed accordingly. Your agency must have the capability to provide or arrange for all four levels, even if most of your patients receive Routine Home Care. Each has different licensing, staffing, and reimbursement implications:

  • Routine Home Care (RHC): This is the most common level of hospice care, provided wherever the patient calls home—be it a private residence, an assisted living facility, or a nursing home. Your interdisciplinary team visits the patient intermittently to provide nursing, aide, social work, and spiritual support.
  • Continuous Home Care (CHC): Provided during periods of medical crisis to manage acute symptoms and avoid hospitalization. This involves skilled nursing care for a minimum of 8 hours in a 24-hour period, with at least half of that care provided by an RN.
  • Inpatient Respite Care (IRC): Short-term care provided in a Medicare-certified facility (like a hospital, hospice facility, or nursing home) to give the patient’s primary caregivers a break. This is limited to five consecutive days at a time.
  • General Inpatient Care (GIP): For pain and symptom management that cannot be handled in any other setting. GIP is provided in a Medicare-certified facility and is intended for short-term use until symptoms are under control and the patient can return home.

Beyond these levels of care, strategic opportunities exist in how you structure your service delivery. The market report highlights a need for residential hospice facilities, which provide a dedicated, home-like setting for patients who cannot or do not wish to remain in their own homes. While capital-intensive, these facilities address significant capacity shortages. Other growth areas include developing a pediatric hospice program, creating specialized programs for dementia and neurological diseases, and offering culturally sensitive services to Minnesota’s diverse communities.

Program size is typically measured by Average Daily Census (ADC). A new agency might start with a target ADC of 10-20 patients and grow from there. Demand is strongest in urban centers like the Twin Cities metro area and other regions with a high concentration of seniors, where there are also more referral sources. However, rural and greater Minnesota areas may offer entry opportunities with less competition, though they come with logistical challenges related to staff travel and service coordination.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Before you can serve patients, you must establish a solid legal and regulatory foundation. Providers typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC) or S-Corporation to protect personal assets from business liabilities. Your initial administrative steps must include:

  • Register your business entity with the Minnesota Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS, which is necessary for hiring employees and tax purposes.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including professional liability (malpractice), general liability, and workers’ compensation.
  • Submit a comprehensive licensing application to the Minnesota Department of Health (MDH).

This application is a significant undertaking. It requires you to submit detailed information about your business structure, key personnel, financial viability (often through a pro forma budget), and, most importantly, a complete set of policies and procedures that demonstrate your ability to comply with state and federal regulations.

The licensing and certification timeline is a multi-stage process that generally ranges from 12 to 18 months. This includes the initial state licensure from MDH, followed by the critical step of seeking Medicare certification. You cannot bill Medicare—the primary payer for over 90% of hospice care—until you are certified. This involves either a direct survey from MDH on behalf of CMS or a survey from a CMS-approved accrediting organization like The Joint Commission, CHAP, or ACHC. This lengthy timeline must be factored into your financial planning and startup budget.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A detailed business plan is your blueprint for success and is essential for securing funding and guiding your operations. Startup costs in Minnesota for a hospice agency typically range from $200,000 to $600,000. This wide range depends on whether you are starting a standard agency with a leased office or developing a capital-intensive residential hospice facility. Key startup expenses include licensing and consulting fees, legal services, office rent and setup, electronic medical record (EMR) software implementation, initial payroll before revenue begins, and funds for marketing and insurance premiums.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by staffing, which typically represents 60-70% of total costs. This reflects the labor-intensive, team-based nature of hospice care. Your financial projections must be built on a clear understanding of reimbursement rates. Typical revenue ranges in Minnesota include:

  • Medicare Reimbursement: Approximately $210 – $350 per day, varying by the level of care provided and the geographic location within the state.
  • Medicaid Reimbursement: Approximately $180 – $320 per day.
  • Projected Revenue (Year 1): A new agency can expect to generate $300,000 – $600,000 as it builds its census.
  • Projected Revenue (Year 3): With established referral networks, revenue can grow to $800,000 – $1,500,000.

Providers operating at a target utilization of 70-80% capacity (based on your staffed Average Daily Census) can generally achieve 10-20% profit margins. Reaching break-even often takes 12-18 months, aligning with the time required to achieve full licensure, Medicare certification, and a stable patient census. Your pro forma financial statements should model various census growth scenarios to understand your cash flow needs during this critical startup phase.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

For a standard hospice agency providing care in patients’ homes, the primary physical location is an administrative office. This office serves as the hub for your interdisciplinary team, record-keeping, and management. It must be professional, secure, and compliant with all relevant regulations. Key facility requirements for an office include:

  • A secure, professional office space compliant with local zoning and accessibility (ADA) laws.
  • A HIPAA-compliant, locked area for storing physical patient records.
  • A secure IT infrastructure and EMR system for managing electronic protected health information (ePHI).
  • A private conference room for confidential Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) meetings and family consultations.
  • Sufficient workspace for your clinical managers, social workers, chaplains, and administrative staff.
  • Secure, climate-controlled storage for medical supplies and any durable medical equipment (DME).

If you are pursuing the strategic opportunity of a residential hospice, the facility requirements are far more extensive and are strictly regulated by the MDH. You will need to design or renovate a facility that feels like a home while meeting institutional health and safety standards. This includes private patient rooms, accessible bathrooms, common areas for families, a kitchen, and specific safety features like call systems and fire suppression.

Location selection is a strategic decision. You should choose a location that is centrally located to the geographic area you intend to serve, minimizing staff travel time. Proximity to key referral sources like major hospitals and medical centers can also be advantageous. Finally, ensure your chosen location is in an area with a sufficient workforce of nurses, aides, and other healthcare professionals.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Your staff is your most valuable asset. The quality of your hospice program is a direct reflection of the skill, compassion, and dedication of your team. Both MDH and CMS mandate a specific Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) that is responsible for the planning and delivery of all patient care. Required roles for a Minnesota hospice typically include:

  • Medical Director (Physician): Oversees the medical components of the hospice plan of care and serves as a resource for the team.
  • Registered Nurse (RN) Case Manager: Manages the overall patient care plan, performs skilled nursing visits, and coordinates the IDG.
  • Licensed Social Worker (LSW): Addresses the patient’s and family’s psychosocial needs, provides counseling, and connects them with community resources.
  • Spiritual Counselor / Chaplain: Assesses and provides for the spiritual needs of the patient and family, regardless of their beliefs.
  • Hospice Aides (CNA): Provide personal care to the patient, such as bathing, dressing, and assistance with daily activities, under the supervision of an RN.
  • Bereavement Coordinator: Manages the bereavement program, providing support to the family for up to 13 months after the patient’s death.
  • Volunteer Coordinator: Recruits, trains, and manages a team of volunteers, who are a required component of a Medicare-certified hospice.
  • Therapists (Physical, Occupational, Speech): Provided as needed to support the patient’s goals for comfort and quality of life.

Training is a critical compliance requirement. All staff must receive comprehensive orientation on the hospice philosophy, pain and symptom management, patient rights, infection control, emergency procedures, and the specific duties of their role. Furthermore, ongoing continuing education is mandated by both MDH and CMS to ensure your team remains current on best practices in end-of-life care. Documenting all training activities is essential for passing surveys.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Comprehensive, well-written policies and procedures are the backbone of a compliant hospice agency. They are not just for passing your initial licensing survey; they are the day-to-day operational guides for your staff. Minnesota and CMS require written policies covering virtually every aspect of your operation. Key areas include:

  • Patient Admission, Transfer, and Discharge Criteria
  • Patient and Family Rights and Grievance Procedures
  • Pain and Symptom Management Protocols
  • Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) Care Planning and Coordination
  • Medication Management and Administration
  • Infection Control and Emergency Preparedness Plans
  • Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI) Program
  • Volunteer Program Management and Utilization
  • Bereavement Care Services for Families
  • Staffing, Supervision, and Training

Individual care plans are the central focus of hospice documentation. The IDG must develop a comprehensive, individualized plan of care for each patient within days of admission. This plan must be reviewed and updated by the full IDG at least every 14 days. This rigorous process ensures that the care provided is responsive to the patient’s changing condition and continues to meet their goals. Your EMR system will be a critical tool for developing, managing, and documenting these care plans in a compliant manner.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Unlike many other businesses, hospice marketing is not about direct-to-consumer advertising. The most successful and sustainable marketing strategy is building strong, trust-based relationships with professional referral sources. Patients and families almost always learn about hospice through a trusted healthcare provider. Your primary referral sources in Minnesota will be:

  • Hospitals and Health Systems (specifically discharge planners, case managers, and palliative care teams)
  • Oncologists and other Specialists (e.g., cardiologists, pulmonologists, neurologists)
  • Skilled Nursing Facilities (SNFs)
  • Assisted Living Facilities
  • Primary Care Physicians
  • Home Health Agencies

Your marketing efforts should be focused on educating these professionals about your agency’s unique strengths. This is often done by a dedicated Hospice Liaison or Community Educator. Their job is to meet with referral sources, explain your services, demonstrate your responsiveness, and prove your commitment to quality care. Success is built on a reputation for excellent communication, seamless admissions, and outstanding clinical outcomes. Focus on being a reliable partner who makes their jobs easier and provides exceptional care to the patients they entrust to you.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Achieving licensure and certification is just the beginning. Ongoing compliance is a constant process. Oversight includes unannounced surveys from the Minnesota Department of Health (MDH) for state licensure and a CMS-approved accrediting organization (like The Joint Commission, CHAP, or ACHC) or MDH on behalf of CMS for Medicare certification. These inspections are rigorous and detail-oriented.

Surveyors will review patient charts, personnel files, policies and procedures, and conduct interviews with staff and families. They focus on ensuring you are following your own policies and meeting every state and federal regulation. Some of the most common deficiencies found during hospice surveys include:

  • Incomplete, inaccurate, or untimely patient care plans.
  • Medication management errors or reconciliation issues.
  • Insufficient or poorly documented IDG meetings.
  • Gaps in the supervision of hospice aides by registered nurses.
  • Failure to follow infection control protocols.

To avoid these pitfalls, you must foster a culture of continuous quality improvement. Your QAPI program should be an active, data-driven process used to identify and correct problems before a surveyor finds them. Maintaining audit-ready documentation at all times is not just a best practice—it is essential for survival and success in the highly regulated hospice industry.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

  • How long does it take to open a Hospice Program in Minnesota?

The entire process, from business planning to receiving your first patient, typically takes 12 to 18 months. This includes the time needed for state licensing with the MDH and the crucial, often lengthy, Medicare certification process which is required to get paid.

  • What licenses are required?

You need a Hospice Program license from the Minnesota Department of Health (MDH), governed by Minnesota Statutes 144A.75. Additionally, to receive payment from the vast majority of patients, you must obtain Medicare certification by passing a rigorous survey from a CMS-approved body.

  • What reimbursement is available?

The primary reimbursement sources are Medicare and Medicaid. Medicare pays a per diem rate ranging from approximately $210 to $350, depending on the level of care (Routine, Continuous, Inpatient, Respite). Minnesota Medicaid (Medical Assistance) rates are similar, ranging from $180 to $320 per day.

Conclusion

Starting a Hospice Program in Minnesota is a challenging but profoundly rewarding venture. It requires careful planning, a deep understanding of state and federal regulations, and unwavering operational discipline. The market holds clear opportunities for providers who can deliver high-quality, specialized care and build strong community partnerships. Providers who invest in compliance, develop a compassionate and skilled team, and cultivate strong referral relationships are positioned for long-term success and the privilege of serving patients and their families at one of life’s most critical moments.
